rashi:a1.1: It should have said “with regard to the male and with regard to the female”: in the language of the verse, as it is written about valuations (Leviticus 27), “if male … if female,” and “son” and “daughter” are not written. But the whole of [the chapter] Yotze Dofen we learned in terms of son and daughter.
rashi:a2.1: And what is different: in valuations, that a female, when she ages beyond sixty, stands at one-third, for the valuation of a young woman is thirty shekels and the valuation of an old woman ten shekels.
rashi:a2.2: And what is different about a male: that when he passes sixty he does not stand at one-third, for the valuation of an old man is less than one-third of the valuation of a young man: a young man is fifty shekels and an old man fifteen shekels.
rashi:a2.3: Paḥa: a broken thing that is good only as a load. Another version: we read paḥḥa, a term for naked and bare, as the Aramaic translation of the Prophets renders “naked” as paḥiaḥ (Ezekiel 16).
rashi:a2.4: Sima: a hidden treasure, for she can exert herself and do work in her old age.
rashi:a4.1: Mishna: One who says: My weight is upon me. [A heading only.]
rashi:a4.2: Yirmatya: the name of the woman.
rashi:a5.1: The weight of my forearm is upon me: how can he weigh it? If he wishes, he presses down and makes it heavy, and if he wishes, he lightens it.
rashi:a5.2: He fills a barrel with water and inserts it: into it.
rashi:a5.3: Up to his marpek: the atzil, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). When he inserts it the water spills out, and when he takes it out the barrel is found lacking.
rashi:a5.4: And he weighs donkey flesh: for the weight of donkey flesh is like the weight of human flesh. And in that flesh there should be sinews and bones in proportion to what is in the arm, since the weight of bones and sinews is not the same as the weight of flesh. And places it into it until it fills: for now there is a volume the size of his arm, and according to that weight he gives.
rashi:a6.1: Gemara. [He may exempt] himself with anything: whatever he wishes to weigh, he weighs.
rashi:a7.2: In a place where they weigh kofra: where they sell pitch by weight.
rashi:a8.2: They throw in two or three: as sellers do.
rashi:a8.3: Its status as weighed is void: and it turns out that they are not sold by weight.
rashi:a9.1: An incident to contradict?: The first clause teaches “if silver, silver,” and so on, and we established that it comes to teach that if he did not specify, he may exempt himself with anything; and then it teaches about the mother of Yirmatya, who said “the weight of my daughter is upon me” without specifying, and she weighed her in gold.
rashi:a11.1: My height: implies like his height, and he gives a thick rod, so thick that he cannot bend it; if he specified silver, silver, and if gold, gold.
rashi:a11.2: My full height: he intended only the measure of the height of his stature, and not its thickness.
rashi:a12.1: Rav Yehuda states it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva. [A heading only.]
rashi:a12.2: Neither the pit: one who sells a house has not sold the pit in it, or the cistern. A bor is dug out without built walls, and a dut is built.
rashi:a12.3: And he must: the seller must buy himself a path from the buyer, to walk through it to that pit and cistern, for he sold him all the land and reserved nothing; since he holds that a seller sells generously.
rashi:a13.1: He need not: for a seller sells grudgingly, and he reserved a path for himself.
rashi:a13.2: When he said to him: the seller to the buyer: I am selling you a house except for these, the pit and the cistern; then he need not buy himself a path. Evidently, since he did not need to specify, for even without specifying the pit and cistern are not included in the house, and he specified, he certainly said it to add something, to let him know that he reserves [a path] for himself. Here too, since “my height” already implies the height of my stature, and he said “full,” evidently he came to add something, to let it be known that he intends only the measure of the height.
rashi:a14.1: Omdi [my standing; the Davidson English renders “my stature”] is upon me: does it imply a rod of his height or not?
tosafot:a4.1: Mishna: One who says: My weight is upon me. [A heading only.]
tosafot:a5.1: Up to his marpek: Rashi explained, the atzil, which is called (an Old French gloss) in the vernacular. This does not seem right, for in the baraita in the Gemara it teaches “up to the atzil,” and it cannot be [what Rashi’s gloss names], for it is stated in the second chapter of Zevaḥim (18b): “They shall not gird themselves with what causes sweat” [Ezekiel 44:18], meaning that they would not gird themselves at a place of sweat, neither below their loins nor above their atzilim, but opposite the atzilim of their arms. And if you say it is [what Rashi’s gloss names], on the contrary, that is a place of sweat. Therefore Ri explained that it is what is called (an Old French gloss) [that is, the elbow, as the Davidson English renders it]. I have discussed this at length in Menaḥot (37a) and in Zevaḥim (19a).
tosafot:a8.1: After they weigh they throw in two or three: And if you ask: everywhere, too, they would give more than the weight, as is evident in Bava Batra, chapter HaMokher et HaSefina (88b); so how could one have thought that the status of weight is void? One may answer that this is the meaning: here it is a place where they weigh and then throw in two or three beyond the [customary] tipping of the scale; therefore one might have thought that it is void, since he gives more than is due.
tosafot:a12.1: He states it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, and so on: It is puzzling: who taught the baraita? Neither Rabbi Akiva nor the Rabbis! For they disagree only in that one master holds that a seller sells generously and the other master holds that a seller sells grudgingly and reserves the path for himself; so according to the Rabbis the superfluous language [“except these”] is not needed. But where the superfluous language is needed, the Rabbis too would surely agree that it is effective. If so, whose view is the baraita?
tosafot:a14.1: In brief: All the dilemmas can be read as a chain of “if you say.” My standing: does he mean a rod that does not bend, or only a rod that can stand, even if it bends? If you say “my standing” lets him give a rod that bends, then my width: does he need a rod truly as wide as he is, which cannot be bent (when he bends his height he does not bend his width), or a rod as long as his width, even if it bends? If you say a rod that bends for width, then my sitting: does it mean without bending, as he sits from his head to his feet, or a bent rod, since a sitting person is bent? If you say sitting means a bent rod, then my thickness: is it a rod as thick as his body, unbent, since his thickness does not bend, or a large rod the full measure of his thickness even if it bends? If you say thickness allows bending, then my girth: a rod that goes around his whole body and is so thick it cannot be unbent, or anything that goes around him, however thin? Rabbeinu Elḥanan explained “my sitting” as either from his head to the place where he sits, half his body, or his whole body as he sits, head to feet; and some explain it as a rod that matches his sitting height rather than his standing height, or a rod that holds the place where he sits. gershom:a1.1: It should have said “with regard to the male and with regard to the female”: as it is written in the Torah, “then your valuation shall be for the male … and if it be a female.” Rather, conclude from it that it is speaking of the chapter Yotze Dofen.
gershom:a2.1: She stands at one-third: as it is written, “from twenty years old until sixty years old … and if it be a female, then your valuation shall be thirty shekels,” and it is written of sixty years and up, “for the female ten shekels,” which is one-third.
gershom:a3.1: The male does not stand at one-third: as it is written, from twenty years old until sixty, fifty shekels, whereas of sixty years and up it is written fifteen shekels, which is less than one-third.
gershom:a4.1: A paḥa in the house: a snare.
gershom:a5.1: A sima in the house: a treasure, who guards everything in the house.
gershom:a6.1: Hadran alakh HaSeg Yad: we will return to you, chapter “Affordability.”
gershom:a7.1: One who says: My weight is upon me: to give to the Temple treasury.
gershom:a8.1: If silver: if he vowed silver, he gives his weight in silver.
gershom:a9.1: Up to his marpek: up to his armpit, which is the shoulder; and as much as he inserts his arm into the barrel, that much water spills out.
gershom:a10.1: And he weighs: he takes donkey flesh, sinews and bones corresponding to the arm and puts them into the barrel until it fills, so that the water rises to the top. Afterward he takes the donkey flesh out; that is the weight of his arm, and according to that weight he gives.
gershom:a11.1: And how is it possible to match flesh with flesh: to put donkey flesh against the flesh and bones against the bone of the arm? Perhaps the bone of the arm is larger than this bone, and it weighs more.
gershom:a12.1: Rather, they appraise the arm: they estimate how much it is likely to weigh, without a weight.
gershom:a13.1: Even with anything: that is, with whatever he wishes that people usually sell by weight.
gershom:a15.1: Who measure: who sell by measure.
gershom:a17.1: They throw in two or three: as an extra, as a bonus.
gershom:a18.1: It teaches us: that it is not void, and he exempts himself with them.
gershom:a19.1: An incident to contradict? In the first clause you said that with “my weight is upon me,” unspecified, he exempts himself with anything, and now you say that she gave her weight in gold.
gershom:a20.1: When she said it without specifying, we assess [the printed text reads “we say”] according to his dignity: if he is wealthy, we assess him by the most precious of the things that are weighed.
gershom:a21.1: My height is upon me: that is, to give the measure of my height in silver or in gold to the Temple treasury.
gershom:a22.1: He gives a rod: of silver, thick, that does not bend by itself, since he said “his height,” meaning something that can stand by itself and does not bend.
gershom:a23.1: My full height is upon me, he gives a rod that bends: that is, since he said “my full height,” he means only that it be as long as I am, even if it is thin.
gershom:a24.1: He states it in accordance with Rabbi Akiva: Rav Yehuda does.
gershom:a25.1: Neither the pit nor the cistern: we learned this about sales in Bava Batra: he has sold neither the pit nor the cistern even though he wrote for him “its depth and its height” of the courtyard; and one might have said that these are part of its depth.
gershom:a26.1: And he must buy himself a path: the seller from the buyer, to walk through to his pit, for a seller sells generously and did not reserve a path for himself.
gershom:a27.1: And the Rabbis say he need not buy himself a path, for a seller sells grudgingly and reserved a path for himself.
gershom:a28.1: And Rabbi Akiva concedes, when the seller said to the buyer, “I am selling you the whole house except the pit and the cistern,” that he need not buy himself a path. What is the reason? Since he did not need to say “except this,” and he said it, he said it in order to reserve a path for himself.
gershom:a29.1: Here too: that is, since he needed to say only “my height is upon me,” and he said “my full height,” he meant something less.
gershom:a30.1: He is coming to add an element: that is, that is why he added to his words. And some say the reverse: “My height is upon me,” he gives a rod that bends; “my full height is upon me,” he gives a rod that does not bend, for all superfluous language comes to add an element.
gershom:a31.1: Omdi, what is the halakha?: if he said “omdi is upon me,” what is the halakha: is this wording the language of vows or not?
rashi:b1.1: My width is upon me, what is the halakha? Does it imply a rod as wide as I am, or does it imply a long rod the measure of my width?
rashi:b1.2: My girth, what is the halakha? Does he give a rod that bends, as long as the measure of his girth, or perhaps he must give a rod as thick as his girth? Let it stand.
rashi:b2.2: Up to the knee: and from there upward it is not “leg” but thigh.
rashi:b5.1: Up to the joint: the place where the palm and the arm join. Evidently yad is only up to the joint, since yad is written in the verse.
rashi:b7.1: The language of people: it is called yad up to the atzil.
rashi:b7.2: Kibbora: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), at the top of the arm, a little distance from the atzil.
rashi:b7.3: Regalim: three pilgrimage Festivals a year.
rashi:b8.1: Excluding those with artificial legs [ba’alei kabbin]: one whose foot was cut off at the first joint near his shin, and he hollows out a kav lined with rags and puts his shin into it, which is called (Rashi adds an Old French gloss). He is exempt from the appearance [at the Temple], since he has no regel. Evidently it is called regel only up to the first joint, which is called (an Old French gloss).
rashi:b10.1: She performed ḥalitza: on one whose leg was cut off and a little of it remained from the knee downward, her ḥalitza is valid. Evidently up to the knee is regel, so let him be obligated in the appearance [at the Temple].
rashi:b11.1: From upon his foot: implies what is upon his foot, that is, the shin, up to the knee.
rashi:b12.1: Conclude from it: since it does not count the shin, up to the knee, as “from upon that which is from upon.”
rashi:b12.2: This istaveira, (Rashi adds an Old French gloss), descends to the ground: for it has only an upper joint, connecting it to the shin, but below it has no joint; rather, it is of a piece with the bone of the sole of the foot. For if it entered your mind that below it too is separate, the istaveira would be, and so on.
rashi:b13.1: Mishna. This is a stringency of vows over valuations: for in valuations, if he said “the valuation of my hand is upon me” or “the valuation of my foot is upon me,” he has said nothing, unless he said it of something on which life depends.
rashi:b14.1: Gemara. The assessment of damages: as one assesses a person whose hand his fellow cut off: they appraise him like a slave being sold in the market, how much he was worth before and how much he is worth now.
rashi:b15.1: There the man is depreciated: for his hand has already been cut off, and even his original value, when they now estimate how much he was worth before, is appraised only cheaply, for they see him as depreciated.
rashi:b15.2: Here the man is of good value: for both his hands are whole, and one must appraise how much he is worth now, since he consecrates his value, and how much he would be worth if his hands were cut off.
rashi:b16.1: His one hand, what is it, and the other is severed?: that is, why does he work with one hand? Because the other is cut off; that is the assessment of damages.
rashi:b16.2: His hand is written over to his first master: so that he may not do work with it for his second master; for now we appraise him as a man of good value.
rashi:b17.1: They assessed him by the assessment of damages: his fellow injured him, and they assessed how much he was worth and how much he is worth.
rashi:b17.2: And he said “my assessment is upon me”: and he did not say “my valuation is upon me.” Must he be appraised again or not?
rashi:b17.3: An assessment by ten: for one who says “my assessment is upon me” is appraised by ten, as we learned in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (2a): land, by nine and a priest, and a person likewise; and the assessment of damages is by three, as we learned: robbery and injuries, by three.
tosafot:b3.1: And he weighs donkey flesh, sinews and bones, and places it into it until it fills: Rabbeinu Elḥanan found this puzzling: since he has already weighed donkey flesh against the weight of his arm, why does he put still more donkey flesh into the barrel? It seemed to him that this is the meaning: he weighs the donkey flesh and sinews once he has put the flesh into the water until it filled; that is, first he puts the flesh into the water until the barrel fills, and afterward he weighs it as the measure of his arm. But I found in the name of Ri that it says “weighs” first deliberately, and afterward he puts it in; not putting it in first, because the water is absorbed into the flesh and makes it heavier than the person’s arm, for a living person carries himself, and the living is lighter than the dead. And it is a stretch to say that they weigh donkey flesh against the arm as it would be if cut off, for it would then weigh more than when it was wholly attached to the body.
tosafot:b8.1: Regalim excludes those with artificial legs: Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: how is it implied from here that regel means only up to the ankle [istaveira]? Perhaps the reason is that he cannot lean on it, even if you call it regel up to the knee; for indeed in the first chapter of Ḥagiga (3a) we also exclude the lame and the blind, because they cannot walk and lean without a staff. And he answered that there in Ḥagiga there are two expositions of “regalim”: from one it excludes the lame and the blind, for the reason that they cannot walk and lean without something, even though they have a leg; and from the other it expounds “regalim, excluding those with artificial legs,” for the reason that he has no leg.
tosafot:b10.1: She performed ḥalitza: where the leg was cut off and a little remained from the knee downward, her ḥalitza is valid; so Rashi. This does not seem right, for in Yevamot (103a) it says that even if she performed ḥalitza for one whose foot was turned backward, her ḥalitza is invalid. Therefore one must explain that it speaks here of where the straps of the shoe are tied: if they were tied from the knee downward it is valid, since this is properly “she removed his shoe from upon his foot”; but if they were tied above, his ḥalitza is invalid, for this is not “from upon his foot.”
tosafot:b15.1: There the man is depreciated: Rashi explained: his hand has already been cut off, and even his original value is appraised only cheaply, since they see him as depreciated. Ri objects to this explanation. First, how is this different from one who vows? The Torah says of the one who vows (Exodus 21:30), “he shall give the redemption of his life,” that he must give his full value; so too with damages, where the verse says to assess his full value, he pays. Second, what is meant below by “and the other is severed; that is the same thing,” namely that they assess the slave’s hand as one who has only one hand and the other cut off, and that this is the same as the assessment of damages? On the contrary, that is not the assessment of damages, for in damages we assess at less than his worth as a whole person, since once his hand was cut off he is repulsive; but here, with the slave, even though one hand is cut off, we still assess by the work of his one hand in full, and he is a man of good value. So Ri explains: Abaye said, is it comparable? There, in damages, the man is depreciated, for once his hand was cut off he is more repulsive than had he a hand that was merely bound, so he must be assessed according to the depreciation; but here, with the one who vows, the man is of good value, for both his hands are whole; therefore they assess him at less than his worth, assessing him as though his hand were written over to the government.
tosafot:b17.1: Or perhaps an assessment by ten is different: as it is taught in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (15a): land [is assessed by nine and a priest], and a person likewise, because ten mentions of “priest” are written in the passage, as Rashi explained. And Rabbeinu Elḥanan asked: why are no more than ten needed? Is this not an evenly balanced court, and any matter that depends on judgment needs a deciding voice? And it is also called a court, and a court is not made even: one more is added to it, making eleven; for of all courts, in monetary and capital cases, it says “a court is not made even; one more is added to them,” in the first chapter of Sanhedrin (2b). [And see further Tosafot on Megilla 23b, s.v. asara.]
gershom:b1.1: Up to the atzil: that is, his marpek.
gershom:b2.1: An allusion to the matter: that donkey flesh is compared to human flesh; therefore they estimate with donkey flesh.
gershom:b3.1: As far as possible: we measure with the water, and what we cannot, we measure by estimate.
gershom:b4.1: And the arm up to the atzil: that is to say, up to the atzil is called yad.
gershom:b5.1: Up to the joint: up to the place where the palm of the hand ends.
gershom:b6.1: With regard to vows, follow the language of people: and people call it yad up to the atzil.
gershom:b7.1: This is the kibborit: which is called (a vernacular gloss). Evidently up to there it is called yad by Torah law.
gershom:b8.1: With regard to vows, follow the language of people: and people call it yad up to the atzil, that is, above the kibborit.
gershom:b9.1: [The editor notes: it seems the text should read, “and that the sanctification of hands and feet is up to the joint is a halakha,” and so on.] And “up to the joint” they learned as a halakha [by tradition].
gershom:b11.1: Regalim excludes those with artificial legs: what is written, “three regalim,” is to say that one who has legs shall go up for the Festival, excluding one who has a leg of wood, that is, kabbin: one hollows out something like a kav and puts his shin into it. But why is he exempt? He still has a leg up to the knee! [The editor notes that here one should mark the answer: “With regard to vows, follow the language of people,”] for up to there people call it regel.
gershom:b12.1: From the knee and below her ḥalitza is valid: evidently up to the knee is called regel by Torah law.
gershom:b13.1: From upon his foot: she may perform ḥalitza on what is above his foot.
gershom:b14.1: Istaveira: which is called (an Old French gloss).
gershom:b15.1: Descends to the ground: and it has no separation down to the end of the heel.
gershom:b16.1: And the shin is “from upon that which is from upon”: the shin is the bone that reaches up to the knee.
gershom:b17.1: This is a stringency of vows over valuations: for in valuations, if he said “the valuation of my hand is upon me,” he has said nothing.
gershom:b18.1: The heirs shall give: for the valuation is fixed in the Torah. [This glosses the mishna’s next line, “a stringency of valuations over vows,” which appears at the top of 20a.]
gershom:b19.1: The assessment of damages: they estimate how much more a person is willing to give for a slave who has another hand than for a slave who has only one hand, as they assess in damages; as we learned: Damage, how so? If he cut off his hand, they view him as though he were a slave being sold, how much he was worth and how much he is worth.
gershom:b21.1: A depreciated man: whose hand is cut off; therefore we assess him as a depreciated man, assessing him as a maimed slave, for since he is maimed he is depreciated and his value is lowered.
gershom:b22.1: Here: one who says “the value of my hand is upon me.”
gershom:b23.1: He is a man of good value: he is a whole person. If they assess him now, how much he is worth whole and how much he is worth maimed, his value comes out high, now that he is still whole. But if they assess him like a maimed man, who is depreciated, how much he is worth now and how much before, his value would be lowered more than if they assess him as himself, whole, and the Temple treasury would lose.
gershom:b24.1: Rather, Abaye said: one assesses him as a whole man, how much a person is willing, and so on.
gershom:b25.1: Who works with one hand, what is that? If you say his other hand is severed, cut off, that is the same as what was said at first, the assessment of damages.
gershom:b26.1: Rather, the other hand is written over to his first master: when his first master sold him, he reserved one of his hands for himself, that he do his master’s work with it; and he is a whole slave.
gershom:b27.1: They assessed him by the assessment of damages: for example, he was injured and they assessed him.
gershom:b28.1: And he said “my assessment is upon me,” what is the halakha? Must he be assessed again, or need he not?
gershom:b29.1: An assessment by ten is different: for in valuations ten people are needed to assess him, since ten mentions of “priest” are written in the passage, while for the assessment of damages a court of three suffices.
gershom:b30.1: Or perhaps he increased in value in the interim: after he was first assessed, and he must be assessed again.
